row.basis: Hebrew זכרון (zikaron, remembrance)
row.note: The commentary makes dhikr both preservation and remembrance; Malachi uses the cognate in a book written for those who fear the Lord and honor his name, joining remembered devotion to a written record.

row.basis: fearers, the Lord's name, book of remembrance
row.note: The commentary says the one who fears will remember and that remembrance of the Lord's name leads to prayer; Malachi's fearers honor the name and are recorded in a book of remembrance.

row.basis: Hebrew זכרון (zikaron, memorial)
row.note: The commentary's dhikr family includes remembrance; here the cognate names a written memorial, giving the word-family a concrete inscriptional use.

row.basis: write as memorial; recite in Joshua's hearing
row.note: The commentary links reminder to written pages and collected recitation; Exodus commands both a written memorial and oral telling, preserving a past event in two forms.

row.basis: Hebrew קרא (qara, read aloud)
row.note: The commentary's q-r-ء family begins with joining words in recitation; Exodus uses the cognate when Moses reads the written covenant aloud to the people.

row.basis: Book of the Covenant read to the people
row.note: The commentary joins recitation to pages; Moses reads a written covenant in the people's hearing, and they answer that they will do its words.

row.basis: guard memory; teach children and grandchildren
row.note: The commentary contrasts preservation with forgetting and commands reminder; Moses warns Israel not to forget what it saw and to pass it to descendants.

row.basis: written song taught to Israel as witness
row.note: The commentary moves from recited revelation to written pages; God tells Moses to write and teach a song so it remains in Israel's mouth as a witness.

row.basis: Book of the Law placed beside the Ark
row.note: The commentary calls Moses' pages a preserved source for the message; Deuteronomy orders the written Law kept beside the Ark as a standing witness.

row.basis: Jeremiah dictates; Baruch writes
row.note: The commentary's reading-to-pages sequence is enacted when Jeremiah speaks God's words and Baruch writes them on a scroll.

row.basis: Jehoiakim cuts and burns the scroll
row.note: The commentary describes deliberate forgetting and a promise that recited words will not be lost; the king deliberately destroys the written words, a sharp counter-scene to that assurance.

row.basis: rewritten scroll with additional words
row.note: After the scroll is burned, Jeremiah dictates again and Baruch writes a replacement with more words; this gives the commentary's movement from loss to recollection and pages a concrete recovery narrative.

row.basis: never forgetting precepts that preserve life
row.note: The commentary says remembrance is the opposite of forgetting and that remembered teaching is kept; the psalmist says God's precepts preserve life and therefore will not be forgotten.

row.basis: lost sheep; seek your servant; I have not forgotten
row.note: The commentary defines recollection as seeking what has gone missing; the psalmist asks God to seek him as a lost sheep while affirming that he remembers God's commandments.

row.basis: one person's guilt is not borne by another
row.note: The commentary cites the principle that no burden-bearer carries another's burden; Ezekiel says children do not bear parents' guilt or parents children's, grounding the same individual accountability in a different legal setting.

row.basis: gather leftover fragments so none is lost
row.note: The commentary pictures forgotten matter as dropped remnants and traces a movement toward gathering; Jesus orders the leftover fragments gathered so that none is lost.

row.basis: searching for a lost coin until it is found
row.note: The commentary defines recollection as seeking what has slipped away; the woman searches carefully for a lost coin, making recovery an active search rather than passive recall.

row.basis: Spirit teaches and reminds disciples of Jesus' words
row.note: The commentary joins divine teaching to the promise of not forgetting; Jesus says the Spirit will teach the disciples and remind them of what he said.

row.basis: recall after the speaker's departure
row.note: The commentary connects reminder with retrieving what has passed and pages that preserve teaching; Peter writes so his readers can recall these things after his death.

row.basis: Scripture announces good news beforehand to Abraham
row.note: The commentary says its message is already in Abraham's and Moses' pages; Paul reads Abraham's promise as Scripture's prior announcement of the gospel to the nations.

row.basis: Moses wrote about Jesus
row.note: The commentary places its present message in Moses' pages; Jesus interprets Moses' writing as testimony about him, a distinct Christian claim about what those pages contain.

row.basis: treasure stored on earth is vulnerable to loss
row.note: The commentary condemns preferring worldly life to what lasts; Jesus warns against storing treasure where moth and rust consume and thieves break in.

row.basis: treasure stored in heaven endures
row.note: The commentary calls the afterlife better and more lasting than worldly life; Jesus contrasts earthly loss with treasure in heaven that is not consumed or stolen.

row.basis: gain the whole world yet forfeit one's life
row.note: The commentary rebukes preference for worldly life in light of the lasting hereafter; Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world at the cost of one's life.

row.basis: world passes; the one doing God's will remains
row.note: The commentary contrasts the preferred worldly life with an afterlife that lasts; John says the world and its desire are passing, while the one who does God's will remains forever.

row.basis: Moses values reward above Egypt's treasure
row.note: The commentary names Moses after rejecting worldly preference; Hebrews says Moses counted reproach greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looked to the reward.

row.basis: each person carries their own load
row.note: The commentary cites the rule that no bearer carries another's burden; Paul says each person will carry their own load, though his surrounding discussion distinguishes this from helping others in trouble.

row.basis: the speakers urge enjoyment of present goods
row.note: The commentary says people prefer present worldly life although the afterlife is more lasting; Wisdom's speakers instead propose enjoying the good things available now, voicing the contrary valuation.

row.basis: forgetting one point of Torah is treated as grave culpability
row.note: The commentary treats forgetting entrusted teaching as loss; this rabbinic reading of Deuteronomy 4:9 makes forgetting a single learned point a serious covenantal offense.

row.basis: Moses is given a written record amid predicted Israelite forgetfulness
row.note: The commentary links revelation, memory and Moses' pages; Jubilees frames a written account given to Moses as a safeguard in a story that anticipates Israel's disobedience and forgetting.

row.basis: forgetting the God who brought Israel out of Egypt
row.note: The commentary explicitly gives forgetting the secondary sense of abandoning God; Deuteronomy warns Israel not to forget the Lord after receiving his commands, making that sense a covenant warning.

row.basis: distinction between those serving God and those not
row.note: The commentary separates the one who fears and remembers from the one who avoids reminder; Malachi says a coming distinction will be made between the righteous and the wicked.

row.basis: God promises not to forget Zion
row.note: The commentary's promise is that the Prophet will not forget the recited message; Isaiah reverses the direction, portraying God as the one who will not forget Zion even if a mother could forget her child.

row.basis: reading the Law with explanation so people understand
row.note: The commentary treats reminder as an aid to recover needed knowledge; Nehemiah describes public reading of the book with explanation that makes its meaning clear to listeners.

row.basis: stirring readers by way of reminder
row.note: The commentary says reminder brings a needed matter back to mind; Peter explicitly describes his writing as stirring readers up by reminding them while he is still alive.

row.basis: ritual meal performed in remembrance
row.note: The commentary places remembrance of the Lord's name immediately before prayer; Jesus tells disciples to repeat a meal in remembrance of him, a distinct Christian liturgical act built around remembrance.

row.basis: hold teaching received by spoken word or letter
row.note: The commentary traces recitation into written pages and notes a root sense of transmitted report; Paul tells the community to hold traditions delivered either orally or by letter.

row.basis: command to bear one another's burdens
row.note: The commentary quotes a rule against one person carrying another's burden; Paul commands mutual burden-bearing, a real ethical counterpoint whose context is helping someone caught in transgression.

row.basis: each person gives an account to God
row.note: The commentary links individual effort with its outcome; Paul says each person will give an account of themselves to God, adding a judgment setting to personal responsibility.

row.basis: visible things are temporary, unseen things eternal
row.note: The commentary contrasts the chosen present life with what endures; Paul distinguishes what is seen and temporary from what is unseen and eternal.

row.basis: the speakers deny return after death
row.note: The commentary affirms an afterlife better and more lasting than present life; Wisdom's speakers argue that death has no return, directly opposing that horizon.

row.basis: Enoch reads heavenly tablets recording human deeds
row.note: The commentary connects prophetic teaching with preserved pages; Enoch is shown written heavenly tablets and reads a record of human deeds, extending the page motif to a celestial archive.

row.basis: Ezra dictates books after the Law has been lost
row.note: The commentary moves from received recitation to gathered pages; 4 Ezra depicts inspired dictation that restores public books after the earlier Law's loss, making preservation through writing central.

row.basis: memory as capacious halls and treasuries
row.note: The commentary pictures memory as a sequence of containers holding what is entrusted; Augustine describes memory as immense halls containing innumerable images, a close account of memory as a storehouse.

row.basis: searching memory for what has been lost
row.note: The commentary defines recollection as seeking what has slipped away; Augustine describes searching memory for a lost item, giving that definition an introspective account.

row.basis: repeating words to children in ordinary daily life
row.note: The commentary moves from received recitation to remembrance; Moses commands repeated teaching at home, on the road, at bedtime and on rising, embedding words in daily memory.

row.basis: words written on doorposts and gates
row.note: The commentary describes written pages as a way to preserve recited teaching; Deuteronomy places the words visibly on household entrances, a distinct public inscriptional form.

row.basis: king writes a copy of the Law from the priests' book
row.note: The commentary connects Moses' pages with a collected written scripture; this law makes the king produce his own copy from the priestly source.

row.basis: king reads the book all his days to learn fear and obey
row.note: The commentary says the one who fears will remember; Deuteronomy ties daily reading of the written Law to fear of God and keeping its words.

row.basis: ancestral deliverance recited in the first-fruits rite
row.note: The commentary links reminder to scripture and worship; the offerer recites a fixed account of Israel's descent to Egypt and deliverance while presenting first fruits.

row.basis: first fruits placed before God with worship
row.note: The commentary places remembrance of the Lord's name before prayer; this liturgy moves from the ancestral recital to presenting the gift and bowing before God.

row.basis: song will not be forgotten by descendants
row.note: The commentary contrasts retained revelation with forgetting; Moses says the taught song will remain in descendants' mouths and testify when later troubles come.

row.basis: Moses finishes writing the whole Law in a book
row.note: The commentary says Moses' pages preserve the message across generations; this verse specifically marks completion of the written book, distinct from its later placement beside the Ark.

row.basis: remember God's works and keep commandments
row.note: The commentary says remembrance preserves teaching; the psalm's intergenerational instruction aims to make children hope in God, not forget his works, and keep his commands.

row.basis: word stored in the heart to prevent sin
row.note: The commentary depicts teaching retained rather than lost; the psalmist says he has stored God's word in his heart so he will not sin.

row.basis: do not forget teaching; let the heart keep commands
row.note: The commentary opposes forgetting to keeping entrusted teaching; Proverbs pairs an explicit command not to forget with the heart's custody of instruction.

row.basis: teaching written on the heart
row.note: The commentary moves between memory and physical pages; Proverbs says to bind fidelity around the neck and write it on the heart, relocating inscription inside the learner.

row.basis: write the oracle on a tablet and in a book as lasting witness
row.note: The commentary carries recited teaching into preserved pages; Isaiah orders a written record for future time, explicitly making inscription a witness that endures.

row.basis: Daniel reads the books and understands Jeremiah's years
row.note: The commentary says the present admonition is already in earlier scriptures; Daniel reads Jeremiah's written prophecy to understand the allotted years, a concrete act of consulting prior pages.

row.basis: prophet eats a scroll, then must speak its words to Israel
row.note: The commentary links divine recitation with a prophet's retention; Ezekiel internalizes a written scroll before being sent to transmit its words to the people.

row.basis: scroll fills the belly and tastes sweet
row.note: The commentary's arc makes written words something received and held; Ezekiel's scroll is taken into his body as nourishment before prophetic speech.

row.basis: prophet finds, eats and delights in God's words
row.note: The commentary connects recitation with remembering the Lord's name; Jeremiah says he found and ate God's words and that God's name was invoked over him, joining reception of words to prophetic identity.

row.basis: word taken from the heart before it is believed
row.note: The commentary contrasts retained reminder with what is lost; in Jesus' explanation of the seed, the devil removes the word from hearers' hearts so they will not believe.

row.basis: cares, riches and pleasures choke the word
row.note: The commentary rebukes preference for worldly life; Jesus says worldly cares, wealth and pleasures choke the heard word before it matures.

row.basis: hearers hold the word fast and bear fruit
row.note: The commentary says the one who fears remembers; Jesus contrasts good soil that holds the heard word fast and bears fruit with the losses in the preceding soils.

row.basis: hearer looks and then forgets what he was like
row.note: The commentary warns that a received thing can be let go; James's forgetful hearer leaves the mirror and immediately forgets, making departure from instruction concrete.

row.basis: persevering doer looks into the law and is blessed
row.note: The commentary links retained remembrance to action; James contrasts the forgetful hearer with one who perseveres in the law and acts, who is blessed.

row.basis: guard the good deposit entrusted to you
row.note: The commentary defines forgetting as failing to keep what was entrusted; Paul tells Timothy to guard the entrusted deposit through the Holy Spirit.

row.basis: Paul delivers what he received, according to Scripture
row.note: The commentary notes a secondary sense of transmitting a report from another; Paul says he handed on what he had received and frames the message as occurring according to Scripture.

row.basis: orderly written account compiled from earlier testimony
row.note: The commentary's q-r-ء discussion presents reading as gathering elements together; Luke says he carefully followed the received accounts and writes them in order.

row.basis: written account meant to establish certainty about teaching
row.note: The commentary's pages preserve what was recited; Luke states that his account is written so Theophilus can know the certainty of what he was taught.

row.basis: books opened; the dead judged by recorded deeds
row.note: The commentary connects earlier pages with each person's own effort and outcome; Revelation depicts the dead judged from opened books according to their deeds.

row.basis: words kept on the heart
row.note: The commentary describes teaching held in memory before it appears on pages; Deuteronomy first places God's words on the heart, the inner counterpart to later visible inscription.

row.basis: God remembers sins no more as an act of forgiveness
row.note: The commentary cites divine forgetting as abandonment of the unfaithful; Jeremiah uses not remembering sins as covenant forgiveness, giving divine non-remembrance an opposite moral valence.

row.basis: Job wishes his words written in a book
row.note: The commentary traces recitation into written pages; Job asks for his own words to be recorded in a book, a lament's appeal for durable preservation.

row.basis: words engraved in rock with iron and lead
row.note: The commentary says the written pages preserve what memory might lose; Job intensifies the wish by asking for words cut permanently into rock.

row.basis: read the Lord's book; none of the creatures is missing
row.note: The commentary says collection prevents the recited word from being dropped; Isaiah directs readers to the Lord's book and claims that none of the listed creatures is absent from its account.

row.basis: those written in the book are delivered in the time of distress
row.note: The commentary joins Moses' pages to the surah's outcomes; Daniel's book records those who will be delivered in a final crisis, linking writing with ultimate fate.

row.basis: joyful reception without roots ends in falling away
row.note: The commentary says a reminder benefits the one who retains it; Jesus describes hearers who receive the word with joy but fall away when tested because it has no root.

row.basis: Timothy has known sacred writings since childhood
row.note: The commentary identifies Moses' pages as a source of teaching; Paul points to Timothy's childhood familiarity with sacred writings and their power to make him wise for salvation.

row.basis: law placed in minds and written on hearts
row.note: The commentary moves between retained memory and pages; Hebrews quotes a covenant promise that God's laws will be placed in minds and written on hearts.

row.basis: community is a letter written by the Spirit on hearts
row.note: The commentary joins human retention to written pages; Paul calls the community a letter of Christ written not in ink but by the Spirit on human hearts.

row.basis: Jesus reads Isaiah's scroll in the synagogue
row.note: The commentary connects recited revelation with prophetic pages; Luke depicts Jesus opening Isaiah's scroll and reading it aloud in a public worship setting.

row.basis: Jesus says the read scripture is fulfilled that day
row.note: The commentary says its message was already present in earlier pages; after reading Isaiah, Jesus interprets the passage as fulfilled in the hearers' present.

row.basis: Law, Prophets and Psalms written about Jesus' suffering and rising
row.note: The commentary asserts that its message is found in Abraham's and Moses' pages; Jesus gives a distinct Christian reading in which the wider scriptural corpus points to his passion and resurrection.

row.basis: John eats a little scroll before receiving a prophetic task
row.note: The commentary's recitation begins with revelation received by a prophet; John takes a written scroll into himself, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach, before being told to prophesy.

row.basis: John is told to prophesy again to many peoples
row.note: The commentary moves received words toward public reminder; after the scroll is eaten, John is commissioned to speak again to many peoples and nations.

row.basis: learning compared to writing on fresh or erased paper
row.note: The commentary connects remembrance with written pages; this rabbinic saying uses the durability of writing on a clean sheet to explain why learning in youth is more firmly retained.

row.basis: Hebrew נשה (nashah, forget), a likely cognate of Arabic نسي
row.note: The commentary develops Arabic n-s-y as forgetting; Joseph names Manasseh because God made him forget hardship, likely sharing the Semitic root, though this is positive relief from suffering rather than forgetting revelation.
